title: Trend Following- How much to Allocate- - Systematic Investor 316

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Trend Following- How much to Allocate- - Systematic Investor 316.docx

speakers: Nick Baltas (quant researcher/trend follower; caption 'Nick Balter')
summary: Nick Baltas and Niels review Aug-Oct 2024 for trend following, then discuss speed in the August V-shaped reversal, three papers on risk-based allocation and carry-optimised trend, and how much to allocate to trend following. Main conclusions: no speed sweet spot, longer lookbacks fare better in real crises, scale by volatility, and size trend by tracking error versus the policy benchmark.

coverage.note: intro; clients defensive after August, less carry appetite
OpenAI, wage settlements, tariffs, China stimulus
commodities in Sept, trend barometer and index numbers, August reflections intro
August equity/currency reversals, risk scaling, FX attribution
speed analysis for V shape, medium speed worst
fixed lookback simulation 20-260 days, speed trade-off
client behaviour after August; S&P/bond/CTA years
Man risk-not-returns paper, volatility predictability, 60/40 risk
dynamic vs static sizing, vol clustering, constrained forecasts
solvency of forecasts, correlation matters for vol target
risk allocation stages, Longtail trend and risk parity

completeness_estimate: 0.85 - the first reader captured the speed/V-shape analysis, three allocation papers and the sizing framework; missed several secondary points (risk-budget reallocation before August, vol-scaling versus signal change, convexity not tested, zero expected return input, EMH discomfort) and made one speaker split error and small date and ranking slips.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: post August we are seeing more and more and more of this defensive mindset coming back
claims.claim: After August 2024 client appetite shifted from carry trades (dominant for about a year and a half) to a defensive mindset, raising interest in trend following.
claims.indicator: client risk appetite carry vs defensive

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: employers were uh at the wheel uh determining terms and now it seems that is changing
claims.claim: Large wage settlements (dock workers 62% over 6 years, Boeing rejecting 30%) signal a shift in labour bargaining power that could spark inflation; EU 45% EV tariffs and higher energy prices add to price pressure.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: this Chinese bazooka that has been uh Unleashed uh which have certainly had an impact on the markets
claims.claim: China's stimulus in Sept 2024 boosted Chinese equities and propagated into commodities such as iron ore after a year of falling prices.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: Commodities as a as a as a whole uh had a very strong um setember
claims.claim: Commodities had a strong September 2024 for different reasons (weather, energy, China) but it was not a great month for systematic commodity strategies.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my Trend barometer at the moment it finished at 36 yesterday so not uh you know not a great reading
claims.claim: Trend barometer 36 on 2 Oct 2024; BTOP50 -78bp in October (+3.34% YTD), SG CTA -92bp (+1.56%), SG Trend about -1% (garbled YTD), short-term traders -63bp (-10bp YTD), MSCI World -1.25% (+16%), global sovereign bonds -8bp (+2.34%), S&P 500 -1% (+19.5%).

correction.issue: Date error: the recording was on Friday 4 October 2024 (the EU EV-tariff vote is reported as 'this morning'), so the barometer reading of 36 'yesterday' was for Thursday 3 October; only the CTA index numbers are 'as of Wednesday night' (2 October).
correction.fix: Niels' trend barometer finished at 36 on Thursday 3 October 2024 (weak); CTA indices as of Wednesday night 2 October: BTOP50 -78bp for October (+3.34% YTD), SG CTA -92bp (+1.56%), SG Trend about -1% for October (YTD garbled), short-term traders -63bp (-10bp YTD); MSCI World about -1.25% (+16% YTD), global sovereign bonds -8bp (+2.34%), S&P 500 about -1% (+19.5%).

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: it does exactly what it says on the team you have been piling on historical Trends year to date equities have been rallying
claims.claim: August 2024 equity reversal and yen/China/Indonesia currency carry unwind hit trend followers who were piling into equity trends, as expected; only equities traded much so dynamic risk scaling overweighted the asset class.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: reversal of the short fixed income trade and for those who use correlations as part of their risk management that would actually lead to equ to the equity exposure being rever or reduced
claims.claim: From Q2 2024 the reversal of the short fixed-income trade, plus correlation-based risk management, reduced equity exposure over the summer before the August reversal.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: currencies including the August reversion have had so far I believe in 2024 the worst year of attribution in a trend program in their history
claims.claim: FX attribution in a trend program in 2024 was the most negative of any calendar year across asset classes in at least 25 years.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: having an average speed which is relatively I guess medium-term 3 to 6 months will get you worse off than being faster than that or slower than that
claims.claim: In the August 2024 V shape a medium-speed trend (3-6 months) did worse than faster or slower speeds: fast speeds participate in fall and recovery, slow speeds barely react, but the middle gets reversed near the trough then misses the rebound. Not a reason to change the model (data mining, false positive).

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it was actually um Co H and what I mean by that was that that downturn was just enough like three or four weeks
claims.claim: In Covid, the 3-4 week downturn was long enough for longer-term models to be short equities and long bonds in time; speed performance depends on the episode, so one cannot conclude a best speed.
claims.indicator: trend speed in Covid vs August 2024

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it not only is it by far the worst look back period
claims.claim: In a 20-year simulation using fixed lookbacks from 20 to 260 days, 20-day trend following was by far the worst, 60-130 days improved a lot and similar, 260 days improved by a big factor; dynamic parameter selection (a cloud of lookbacks) improved further. Short-term trading can be profitable but short-term trend following probably is not.

correction.issue: The condition 'gross of full costs' is unsupported: Niels says only that the 20-year fixed-lookback result is a simulation subject to the usual disclaimers; costs are discussed afterwards as a general trade-off by Nick, not as a statement about this simulation.
correction.fix: Same claim, with condition 'simulated 20-year result, subject to simulation disclaimers; treatment of costs not stated'.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: the quicker you are then you have more false false positives
claims.claim: Choice of speed is a trade-off: slower means less reactivity (missing turning points), faster means more false positives and higher costs, and going faster requires strong cost control.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: static position sizing would have helped because you wouldn't have reduced your Equity exposure throughout that vshape
claims.claim: Static position sizing would have helped in the August 2024 V shape because exposure would not be reduced into the trough, but this is data mining and not a lesson.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the longer you go um you actually get more performance during those uh periods where there is equity crisis
claims.claim: Longer lookbacks give more performance in meaningful, long equity crises; short-lived dips are too quick for trend following, which is the price of long-term compound growth, and overthinking models to remove bad periods ends badly.
claims.indicator: trend lookback vs equity crisis protection
claims.direction: longer lookback better in long crises

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: This is precisely the space that maybe require some contractual protection
claims.claim: Short moves of a day, two days or two weeks are not trend following's domain; combining options protection with trend following is possible but more expensive.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: post August we've seen none of our um I guess um business activities or if you like discussions uh leading to any particular challenge
claims.claim: After August 2024 no clients unwound their trend allocations; asset owners understand that long-term sustained drawdowns, not V shapes, are where trend following pays.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: what are the three worst kalada years of S&P since 2000
claims.claim: The worst S&P years since 2000 were 2002, 2008 and 2022, the worst bond year was 2022, and the best CTA years were 2022, 2014, 2008 (2002 close), showing CTAs pay off in equity and bond stress years.
claims.indicator: calendar-year S&P, bonds and CTA returns

correction.issue: Misstates the best CTA years. After Niels guessed 2022, 2014 and 2008, Nick says depending on the index variant 2002 is one of the top three and 2014 is the fourth ('those three plus one').
correction.fix: Worst S&P years since 2000 were 2002, 2008 and 2022 (2022 also the worst bond year; GFC among the best bond years); the best CTA years were 2008, 2022 and (depending on index variant) 2002, with 2014 fourth.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: risky business why the smart money forecast risk not returns
claims.claim: Man Group paper 'Risky Business: why the smart money forecasts risk not returns': CTAs are first and foremost risk managers; returns cannot be forecast but risks can.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: there is no association between today's realization of volatility and tomorrow's returns
claims.claim: In 100 years of stock data volatility clusters and persists, but today's volatility has no short-term forecasting power for returns while predicting tomorrow's volatility; high risk with down markets implies positive returns only over 1-5 year horizons.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: in a 640 portfolio it ends up being 90% Equity risk and 10% Bond risk
claims.claim: A 60/40 portfolio carries about 90% equity risk and 10% bond risk, and in down markets risk rises without compensation, while the stock-bond correlation turned positive in 2022; hence scale exposure as a function of realised volatility.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: even by just reducing the exposure in a in in in a vol Spike you somehow implicitly play a trend
claims.claim: Reducing exposure in a vol spike implicitly plays a trend; early trend followers used static sizing, but technology allows dynamic sizing.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it is sometimes difficult to tell the difference once you zoom out a little bit between uh the two
claims.claim: Most bigger managers use dynamic position sizing, but long-term returns of static and dynamic managers are hard to tell apart, as is 500 vs 50 markets; Niels does not buy that 500 markets is better than 50.
claims.indicator: static vs dynamic sizing, number of markets

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: volatility beyond the fact that it's clustering it's also mean revering
claims.claim: Volatility clusters and mean reverts, so over long horizons static and dynamic exposure converge, but scaling by volatility matters locally around turning points; spikes have shown negative association with subsequent returns.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: if you constrain your model to only predict positive numbers otherwise you should scrap your prediction
claims.claim: Return prediction models constrained to positive forecasts look better over the long run (equity returns are positive by design) but may not keep the investor solvent at the times returns are negative.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: in a risk parity World correlation only matters for the top level leverage if we have a vol Target
claims.claim: In a risk parity setup correlation only matters for top-level leverage under a vol target; when stocks and bonds correlate positively (2022) volatility overshoots, so incorporate correlation if it is not too noisy.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: they say how about you have a vol Target which in itself allows you to scale the exposures inversely to V
claims.claim: The paper moves from nominal allocation to a vol-targeted risk allocation with a top-level leverage adjustment, reducing vol of vol.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: nominal allocation long-term risk allocation as they call it static and then um active risk allocation
claims.claim: Three stages: nominal allocation, static long-term risk allocation, then active risk allocation using realised volatilities and correlations, which performs best, similar to risk parity.
claims.indicator: nominal, static risk, active risk allocation

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: hey Trend following can help you and they go into this journey of like adding Trend following
claims.claim: A Longtail Alpha paper shows adding trend following to a risk parity stock-bond portfolio helps, particularly in 2022, but replacing bonds with trend following over the long term gives a similar or worse portfolio.
claims.indicator: trend following overlay on risk parity
claims.direction: add trend, do not replace bonds

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: do not go long appreciating markets that have negative carry do not go short depreciating markets that have positive carry
claims.claim: A carry-optimized trend program avoids shorting bonds with positive carry (upward term structure) and longing negative-carry markets, avoiding pre-2022 carry drag while still benefiting in 2022; adding commodities to stocks/bonds raises diversification but drops Sharpe unless carry filtered.
claims.direction: skip trends that pay negative carry

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: this is exactly what I mentioned earlier on trying to be too clever and adding stuff to a trend following model
claims.claim: The carry-optimized trend benefit is based on 1998-2023, exactly when the carry regime started, so the enhancement may overfit; the next 20 years may differ (e.g. rates at 25%) and purity is more robust.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: one of the more successful inflation Hedges is to go short bonds you go short equities and you go long Commodities
claims.claim: An inflation hedge is short bonds, short equities, long commodities, which means paying equity risk premium, term premium and negative roll yield; trend following lets you be dynamic around these.
claims.direction: short bonds, short equities, long commodities

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: longer term Trend followers would not be able to make money when interest rate started to go up
claims.claim: Roy Niedhoefer's 2014 paper argued trend followers would struggle when rates rise; instead shorting bonds became profitable, showing no one knows the future.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: conventional ways of determining sizing do not work
claims.claim: Conventional sizing (mean-variance optimisation) does not work for deciding how much to allocate to trend following; the 2019 paper and a recent large-CTA paper reach the same conclusion.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: any minan variance analysis would tell you to do 70% Trend following 30% the remaining of your portfolio
claims.claim: Mean-variance analysis would put about 70% in trend following because its historical Sharpe is higher than a stock-bond portfolio; minimising downside risk gives about 52% (1999-2019 data), both too high for institutions.
claims.indicator: mean-variance optimisation allocation to trend following

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: anything you do away from it is an active risk decision
claims.claim: Sizing must balance benchmark-relative active risk (tracking error to the policy portfolio) against benefits, since institutions are judged against a benchmark.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: what you really have to assess is a scenario analysis and value ad of various increments of TR following allocation
claims.claim: Assess scenario analysis for increments of trend allocation (2%, 5%, 10%, 15%) with tracking error against benchmark; larger sizes improve tail, Sharpe and downside but carry career risk, and the horizon (1 vs 10 years) changes the value.
claims.indicator: trend allocation increments and tracking error

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: maybe the Strat allocation should change and contain maybe five or 10% or 20% of trend following
claims.claim: Include trend following inside strategic asset allocation (5-20%) so the benchmark absorbs the tracking error.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: maybe 40% in bonds is way too risky today compared to what it was 20 years ago
claims.claim: High government debt levels may make a 40% bond allocation too risky; the 60/40 was a carry trade plus yield reduction at a turning point.

correction.issue: Wrong speaker for part of the claim. Niels makes the debt-level point (40% in bonds may be too risky); the closing remark that 60/40 was a carry trade and a yield reduction at a turning point is Nick agreeing, and he asks which of those components can still exist.
correction.fix: Niels: high government debt levels should be part of why 40% in bonds is too risky today. Nick (agreeing): 60/40 worked as a carry trade plus falling yields at a turning point, and it is an open question which of those components can persist.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: the fact that this report became again relevant for a good amount of our clients is precisely the consequence of those questions now being asked much more
claims.claim: Asset owner interest in trend following and challenging 60/40 has risen since 2022 as bond risk was realised.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: getting closer to August and reversion of those rates moves you ended up reducing the rates exposure and then just before the the reversion INE equities uh you ended up kind of allocating a bit more to equities
claims.claim: Correlation-aware risk management cut equity risk in May-June while the short bond trade was reversing (two positively correlated longs), but as rates exposure was reduced approaching August the freed risk budget went back into equities just before the August reversal, so a risk-budget rule can add to the position that is about to reverse.
claims.indicator: correlation-based risk budgeting between equity and bond trend positions
claims.direction: equity exposure cut May-June then raised before the August 2024 reversal
claims.testable: yes - replay the risk-budget path through June-August 2024

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: they reduced they reduced risk mainly because of vol expansion not so much about the signal making a change for those few days
claims.claim: In the very fast August 2024 reversal, trend models cut exposure mainly through volatility scaling (volatility expansion), not through the trend signal changing within those few days.
claims.indicator: volatility-scaled position size versus trend signal
claims.direction: positions reduced by vol expansion, not signal flips
claims.conditions: very short sell-off with a V-shaped recovery
claims.testable: yes - decompose exposure change into vol-scaling and signal components

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: how you had handled the Yen the Nik over the summer months because there were signs of a change in direction or at least there were signs of those Trends being challenged
claims.claim: Results in the August 2024 reversal depended on how the yen and Nikkei positions had been handled over the summer, since those trends were already being challenged and were weaker than earlier in the year.
claims.indicator: yen and Nikkei trend strength, summer 2024
claims.testable: yes - attribute August 2024 P&L to yen and Nikkei positioning

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: looking into August on a month that the market was positive doesn't even appear if you do your typical kind of Scar plot with a trend following smile
claims.claim: August 2024 was not a test of trend following's convexity (the 'smile' scatter of trend returns against equity returns): the downturn was too short-lived and the month ended positive, so convexity would only have paid if the move had been contagious and a fast model had reacted.
claims.indicator: trend-following smile (CTA returns vs equity returns)
claims.conditions: convexity needs a sustained, contagious downturn
claims.testable: yes - scatter of monthly CTA vs equity returns, label August 2024

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there are more people who are now serious and who want to dive deeper into these type of strategies
claims.claim: August 2024 was a non-event for allocators, but events like 2022 opened discussions, so more asset owners are now serious about trend strategies and willing to act on their research.
claims.testable: partly - flows into CTA / trend products

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: if you ask me I'm going to tell you zero because I have no clue and it shouldn't work in the first place
claims.claim: Asked what expected return to put into a mean-variance optimiser for trend following, Nick would say zero (no ex ante basis and it should not work in theory); yet using its historical Sharpe gives about 70% allocation, so optimiser inputs for trend are either unusable or absurd, which is why a different sizing method is needed.
claims.indicator: expected return input for trend following in mean-variance optimisation
claims.testable: partly - the optimiser output is a calculation; the zero input is a judgement

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: people that don't feel comfortable about following is because it goes against their premises and their fundamental understanding of the market that you know past return should not predict future return
claims.claim: Citing Andrew's point: discomfort with trend following comes from the efficient-market premise that past returns should not predict future returns, but the empirical fact that they do cannot be ignored.
